title: I ported a 1990 Amiga game (Saint Dragon) to the browser from just the floppy image, with no source code. Postmortem inside.
author: lordscanline
selftext:
Hi all!

I wanted to share an AI gamedev experience I had, though this one is more of an AI game *port*: **Saint Dragon**, a semi-obscure Amiga shmup I loved as a kid, rebuilt as a native HTML/JS browser game.

The fun part is that there was no source code, no original assets and no documentation. All I had was the floppy disk images, for a 35-year-old architecture (a famous one, at least, with some very good emulators out there).

I started from an **ADF** and an **IPF** of the original disk. An ADF is a logical copy: the bytes as the OS sees them. An IPF is a lower-level copy of the floppy's magnetic track layout (I'm oversimplifying), so it can preserve copy-protected disks. That matters because floppies had very little space, and crackers often cut things from games to fit their crack on the disk. Saint Dragon also used Rob Northen's **CopyLock** protection, which an ADF can't represent.

I did the port with Claude, plus a lot of my own old Amiga knowledge. First we built a partial Amiga emulator (68000 CPU, Copper, Blitter, Paula audio, disk DMA). It doesn't ship with the game. We used it as a microscope to run the original, inspect the hardware state and check the port against it. Highlights:

* **Disk decoding:** We wrote IPF → MFM → custom track decoders. All **82/82 tracks pass the game's own checksum**, so the original game itself accepted our reconstruction. We passed CopyLock's first stage authentically, and the emulator had to support `ILLEGAL` instructions as control flow, because CopyLock uses them that way.
* **Our first big failure:** We tried grabbing sprites at runtime from the emulator. The backgrounds came out full of enemies and "DEMONSTRATION" text, frames were missing, and one "player" sprite turned out to be an enemy. We threw away about a third of the work and switched to decoding the resource format directly. The rule became: **disk data is the source of truth, and screenshots are only for verification.**
* **Assets:** We decoded all 85/85 resources (custom RLE, planar graphics), which gave 685 sprite objects, 10 palettes, backdrops and parallax strips. One sneaky bug: large sprites are "chained" records, and indexing them wrong produced dozens of unrelated wrong sprites. We did this basically by matching the daat structure and its field to the actual data field.
* **Full disassembly:** We classified **538/538 routines and all 2,891 call sites**, which turned a byte soup into a navigable call graph.
* **A 1990 coroutine engine:** This was surprising and unexpected, but each enemy runs on its own stack with context switching, in a small game from the end of the 80s, early 90s. That maps almost 1:1 onto **JavaScript generators**, so the enemy scripts were transcribed nearly line by line.
* **Hidden wave language:** All enemy spawns come from 602 six-byte records triggered by scroll distance. For a long time we thought there was no spawn data. There was, we just hadn't found the cursor reading it.
* **Collision:** The game uses a double-buffered 64×32 bit grid, where bullets stamp bits and enemies consume them. Basically a hand-rolled spatial hash from 1990.
* **Audio, the hardest part:** The instruments are actual 68000 programs, not samples, and three attempts to resynthesize them failed. What worked was running the original audio driver in the emulator, logging every write to the Paula chip, and replaying that register stream in the browser. The stage theme comes out at 98.3 s, exactly what the decoded score data predicts.
* **Result:** Intro, title, all 5 stages and bosses, music and SFX, checkpoints, ending, high scores, plus keyboard and touch controls to make it mobile friendly.

**Where AI shined and where it didn't:** Claude was amazing at searching thousands of assembly lines, translating routines, writing probes and audit tools, and never getting tired. It was weak at guessing meaning from appearances: plausible labels like "this is the dragon sprite" or "this is the palette" were often wrong. The loop that worked was:

>I spot a concrete mismatch ("this enemy enters from the wrong side") → targeted code search → small fix → executable check → I confirm by playing.

My memory of the original game (and WinUAE running beside it) was the final test, and Claude supplied the bandwidth.

If you want all the gory details (bugs, wrong turns, validation strategy), the full postmortem is here: [https://waldtier.com/games#saint-dragon](https://waldtier.com/games#saint-dragon)

What I was able to do with Claude really amazed me, and it's what got me back into gamedev this year. 20+ years ago I made a lot of small games and mods for UT99, Deus Ex and so on, nothing professional.

Bonus: working this closely with the dragon’s chained-body code gave me the idea for a new game, Vertebra, a shmup roguelite where your tail is your build. It’s playable here: [https://waldtier.itch.io/vertebra](https://waldtier.itch.io/vertebra)

Happy to answer questions!

comments.author: NikopikVR
comments.body: How long did it take you to do this, and was your 100$ suscription enough to do it?
